feedback.problem:
Find the Laplace transform of $y(t),$ if 

$$
{y}^{″}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the scalar multiplication property of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}} & =L{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\ L{{y}^{″}} & =2L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce $L{y}=Y(s).$ 

To calculate $L{{y}^{″}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a second derivative:

$$
L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}L{y}-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)
$$

Taking into account the given initial conditions, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}Y(s)-s.\end{aligned}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}} & =2L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s)-s & =\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s) & =\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+1}+s \\ {s}^{2}Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{3}+3s}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{3}+3s}{{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+1)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+3}{s({s}^{2}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$
